name: Palladas of Alexandria
bio: Palladas of Alexandria was a grammarian and the last great epigrammatist of pagan Alexandria, known for bitter, satirical verse. The editor dates him to the fourth century AD; Paton's index says the fifth.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him.

poems.title: Book V, 71
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Zenon, since you have married the daughter of Protomachus (first in fight) and of Nicomache (conquering in fight) you have war in your house. Search for a kind seducer, a Lysimachus (deliverer from fight) who will take pity on you and deliver you from Andromache (husband-fighter) the daughter of Protomachus.

poems.title: Book V, 72
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: This is life, and nothing else is; life is delight ; away, dull care! Brief are the years of man. To-day wine is ours, and the dance, and flowery wreaths, and women. To-day let me live well; none knows what may be to-morrow.

poems.title: Book V, 257
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Now I condemn Zeus as a tepid lover, since he did not transform himself for this haughty fair’s sake. She is not second in beauty to Europa or Danae or tender Leda. But perhaps he disdains courtesans, for know they were maiden princesses he used to seduce.

poems.title: Book VI, 60
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Pamphile, in place of an ox and a golden offering, dedicated to Isis these glossy locks ; and the goddess takes more pleasure in them than Apollo in the gold that Croesus sent him from Lydia.

poems.title: Book VI, 61
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: O heavenly razor, happy razor with which Pamphile shore her plaited tresses to dedicate them. It was no human smith that wrought thee, but beside the forge of Hephaestus the bright-snooded Grace (to use Homer’s words) took up the golden hammer and fashioned thee with her own hands.

poems.title: Book VI, 85
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: His breaster and leggers and shield and spear and heller Captain Gordy dedicates to Timothy.

poems.title: Book VII, 607
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Old Psyllo, grudging her heirs, made herself her own heir and with a quick leap went down to the house of Hades, contriving to end her life and her outlay at the same time. Having eaten up all her fortune, she perished together with her spending power, and jumped to Hades when her last penny was gone.

poems.title: Book VII, 610
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: One carried off a bride and Fate carried off the wedding party, despoiling of life the merry company. One wedding sent four and twenty corpses to their graves, and one chamber became their common mortuary. Penthesilea, unhappy bride, Pentheus bridegroom of sorrow, rich in deaths was your marriage!

poems.title: Book VII, 681
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: You did not go abroad for the sake of honour, but of death, and although lame you ran to Hades, Gessius, swifter than the Fates. For you retreated from life owing to the advancement of which you were dreaming.

poems.title: Book VII, 682
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Gessius did not die hurried by Fate, but arrived in Hades before Fate.

poems.title: Book VII, 683
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The wisest of the Seven Sages said “Naught in excess,” but you, Gessius, were not convinced of it, and came to this end. Though erudite, you incurred the reproach of the greatest lack of reason in desiring to ascend to heaven. Thus it was that Pegasus was fatal to Bellerophon, because he wished to learn the rules of motion of the stars. But he had a horse and the confident strength of youth, whereas Gessius could not screw his courage up enough even to ease himself.

poems.title: Book VII, 684
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Let no mortal even seek to be a god also, nor pursue the pride of high office. Gessius is the proof of it, for he was first of all puffed up and then collapsed, not content with mortal, felicity.

poems.title: Book VII, 685
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: You sought and found the end of life and happiness, seeking an office tending to the highest end. But you obtained the honour, Gessius, receiving after your death the insignia of office.

poems.title: Book VII, 686
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: When Baucalus saw Gessius just after his death, and lamer than ever, he spoke thus: “Gessius, what made thee descend into Hell, naked, without funeral, in new burial guise?” And to him in great wrath Gessius at once replied: “Baucalus, the pride of wealth may cause death.”

poems.title: Book VII, 687
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: When Gessius discovered the fraud of the oracle of Ammon not long before his death in a strange land, he blamed his own belief and that science, and those who trust in silly astrologers.

poems.title: Book VII, 688
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The two soothsayers brought death on Gessius by their oaths, promising him the consular chair. O race of men vain minded, angry with themselves, knowing nothing even until the end of life.

poems.title: Book IX, 5
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: This pear-tree is the sweet result of the labour of my hand, with which in summer I fixed the graft in its moist bark. The slip, rooted on the tree by the incision, has changed its fruit, and though it is still a pyraster below, it is a fragrant-fruited pear-tree above.

poems.title: Book IX, 6
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I was a pyraster; thy hand hath made me a fragrant pear-tree by inserting a graft, and I reward thee for thy kindness.

poems.title: Book IX, 119
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If a man who is a ruler choose to put up with flatterers, he will sacrifice many to their vile mouths ; so the best men, in righteous hatred, should detest the flattered as much as the flatterer.

poems.title: Book IX, 165
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Woman is the wrath of Zeus, given to men in the place of fire, a grievous exchange. For she burns up and withers man with care, and brings hasty old age on youth. Even Zeus does not possess Hera of the golden throne unvexed; indeed he hath often cast her out from the immortals to hang in the mist and clouds; Homer knew this, and hath described even Zeus as being wrath with his wife. Thus never is a woman at concord with her husband, not even when she lies beside him on a floor of gold.

poems.title: Book IX, 166
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Homer shows us that every woman is wicked and treacherous; be she chaste or a whore, in either case she is perdition. Helen’s adultery caused the murder of men, and Penelope’s chastity caused death. All the woes of the Iliad were for the sake of one woman, and Penelope was the cause of the Odyssey.

poems.title: Book IX, 167
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Zeus, in place of fire, bestowed another fire, woman. Would that neither woman nor fire had come into being! Fire, it is true, is soon put out, but woman is a fire unquenchable, flaming, ever alight.

poems.title: Book IX, 169
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The wrath of Achilles was the cause of pernicious poverty to me too, since I adopted the profession of a grammarian. Would that that “wrath” had killed me with the Greeks, before the bitter hunger of grammar had put an end to me. But all to let Agamemnon run away with Briseis, and Paris with Helen, I have become poor.

poems.title: Book IX, 170
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I chastened my shameless belly by severe reasoning, correcting the troublesome gut by temperance. Indeed, if my intellect is in a higher place than my belly, how can I fail to subdue the inferior one of the two?

poems.title: Book IX, 171
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I am selling the implements of the Muses, the books that have made me groan so much, now that I am taking to another profession. Farewell, ye Muses. I bid thee good-bye, Learning, for syntax is the death of me.

poems.title: Book IX, 172
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I care no longer for either Hope or Fortune ; their deceit is now of no account to me; I have reached the haven. I am a poor man, but freedom is my house-mate, and I turn my back on wealth which insults poverty.

poems.title: Book IX, 173
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The beginning of grammar ! is a curse in five lines. The first has the word “wrath,” the second “pernicious,” and after that “many woes” of the Greeks ; the third “leads down souls to Hades”; to the fourth belong “spoil” and “dogs”; to the fifth “birds” of ill-omen and the “anger of Zeus.” How, then, can a grammarian avoid having many sorrows after five curses and five cases (falls) ?

poems.title: Book IX, 174
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The teachers here are those men with whom Sarapis is angry; they start from “pernicious wrath.” Here the nurse brings, perforce, the fee once a month, tying up the wretched pittance in byblus and paper, and puts the contemptible little paper, like a pinch of incense, by the master’s seat, as if by a tomb, She steals some of the small fee and changes the coins, substituting leaden ones, and she receives her commission, If any one agrees to pay a gold coin for a whole year, he changes his teacher in the eleventh month before paying up, and is so ungrateful as to make fun, too, of his former master after robbing him of a whole year’s fee.

poems.title: Book IX, 175
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I sett Callimachus and Pindar, and all the cases in the grammar, being myself a sore case of poverty, For Dorotheus has cut off the salary that supported me, sending this impious message of complaint against me. But, dear Theo, protect me, and do not let me end my days in conjunction with poverty.

poems.title: Book IX, 176
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I was invited to dinner by you, the orator, and if I failed to come I have the honour you paid me, and am still more your friend. For my heart does not rejoice in appreciation of viands, but is nourished only by the honour it tastes.

poems.title: Book IX, 180
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.note: Paton: This and the three following are written on the subject of a Temple of Fortune converted into a Tavern.
poems.text: Fortune, who pliest thy trade through all our life, whose nature is like untempered wine, thou who art ever mixing and pouring from vessel to vessel, now hast thou too become a tavern-keeper instead of a goddess, a calling suitable to thy character.

poems.title: Book IX, 181
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Times are turned topsy-turvy as I see, and we now see Fortune in misfortune.

poems.title: Book IX, 182
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: And thou, Lady Fortune, how has evil fortune befallen thee? How hast thou, who givest us good fortune, become unfortunate? Learn thou, too, to support thy own changes of tide, learn to suffer the unhappy falls which thou sendest to others.

poems.title: Book IX, 183
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: And of thee too, Fortune, they make mockery now thou art changed, and at the end thou hast not even spared thy own fortune. Thou who hadst once a temple, keepest a tavern in thy old age, and we see thee now serving hot drinks to mortals. Justly bewail thine own mischance, fickle goddess, now that thou reversest thine own fortune like that of mortals.

poems.title: Book IX, 377
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Tantalus ate nothing, for the fruit of the trees that tossed over his head ever eluded him, and owing to this, being in want of food, he was less thirsty ; but suppose he had eaten ripe figs, and plums, and apples, do dead men get so very thirsty from eating fresh fruit? But we guests eat all sorts of salted dishes, quails and cheese and goose’s fat, poultry and veal, and on the top of all drink only one glass. So we are worse off than you, Tantalus.

poems.title: Book IX, 378
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: They say that Sarapis appeared in a dream by night to a murderer who was sleeping under a decayed wall, and thus spoke as in an oracle: “Arise, thou who liest here, and seek, poor wretch, another sleeping place.” The man awoke and departed, and immediately the rotten wall fell to the ground. The evil-doer rejoiced, and in the morning sacrificed to the gods in thanks for his escape, thinking that Sarapis is pleased with murderers. But Sarapis appeared to him again at night, and prophesied thus to him: ‘“‘Wretch, dost thou think that I protect criminals? If I did not let thee be killed now, it is that thou now hast escaped a painless death; but know that thou art reserved for the cross.”

poems.title: Book IX, 379
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The proverb says, “Even a pig would bite a bad man;” but I say that we should not say that, but “Even a pig would bite simple unmeddlesome men, but even a snake would be afraid to bite a bad man.”

poems.title: Book IX, 393
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: No magistrate ever came here who was both clean-handed and mild; for the one principle seems antagonistic to the other. Mildness is a virtue of the thief, and purity a virtue of the proud. These qualities are the two instruments of government.

poems.title: Book IX, 394
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: God, father of flatterers, son of pain and care, it is fear to have thee and pain not to have thee.

poems.title: Book IX, 395
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Odysseus said “nothing is sweeter than a man’s fatherland,” for in Circe’s isle he never ate cheese-cake. If he had seen even the smoke curling up from that, he would have sent ten Penelopes to the deuce.

poems.title: Book IX, 397
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: A Spartan once was flying from the battle, and his mother, uplifting a sword to smite his breast, exclaimed: “If thou livest, thou dost fix on thy mother eternal disgrace, and dost violate the inherited laws of mighty Sparta. But if thou dost perish by my hand, they will call me an unlucky mother, but saved from disgrace together with my country.”

poems.title: Book IX, 400
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Revered Hypatia, ornament of learning, stainless star of wise teaching, when I see thee and thy discourse I worship thee, looking on the starry house of the Virgin; for thy business is in heaven.

poems.title: Book IX, 401
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Nature, loving the duties of friendship, invented instruments by which absent friends can converse, pens, paper, ink, handwriting, tokens of the heart that mourns afar off.

poems.title: Book IX, 441: On a Statue of Heracles
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I marvelled seeing at the cross-roads Jove’s brazen son, once constantly invoked, now cast aside, and in wrath I said: “Averter of woes, offspring of three nights, thou, who never didst suffer defeat, art to-day laid low.” But at night the god stood by my bed smiling, and said: “Even though I am a god I have learnt to serve the times.”

poems.title: Book IX, 484
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Odysseus once, when sailing on the sea, received as a gift a bag of winds—a very valuable thing. But this my Aeolus of the windy heart sends me a fowl stuffed with wind. You send me winged winds, my friend, yes wind, and I can’t eat compressed air.

poems.title: Book IX, 486
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: When my slave untied the paunch! you sent me, after tying it up yourself, he found it to be a bellows full of air.

poems.title: Book IX, 487
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: You served me the food of fig-fattened pigs from Cyprus, dry and thirst-provoking. But when you find me sufficiently fig-fattened, either kill me at once or quench my thirst with Cyprian wine.

poems.title: Book IX, 489
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: A grammarian’s daughter, having known a man, gave birth to a child which was masculine, feminine, and neuter. ;

poems.title: Book IX, 502
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I require “conditum.”! Where did “conditum” get its name from for it is alien to the Greek - tongue. If it is a Latin word you will know, who are such a good Latin scholar. Prepare it for me, then, for the malady of the stomach from which I suffer requires this drink, I am told.

poems.title: Book IX, 503
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I was not wrong in saying that there is a divine virtue in dzzyphi. The other day at least I applied a dizyphos to one suffering from a chronic quartan ague, and he became at once as fit as a dog-tick.

poems.title: Book IX, 508
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If one wishes to enjoy a happy day, meeting you makes his day a good one; but if one wishes the contrary, not meeting you makes it a bad one:

poems.title: Book IX, 528: On the House of Marina
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The inhabitants of Olympus, having become Christians, live here undisturbed; for here they shall not be put on the fire in the melting-pot that produces necessary small change.

poems.title: Book IX, 773
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The smith transformed Love into a frying-pan, and not unreasonably, as it also burns.

poems.title: Book IX, 168
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I, unhappy man, have married a wife who is “pernicious wrath,” and my profession, too, obliges me to begin with “wrath.” Oh, man of much wrath, forced to consort with wrath in two things, my calling as a grammarian and my combative wife!
